suggestion_body: Design roles require visual proof. Ensure your primary portfolio link (website, Behance, or Dribbble) is prominent in the header.
Ensure your background and text colors maintain at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for accessibility and readability.
Don't just show the final design. Briefly describe your design thinking process and the problem you solved.
Use a clear typographic hierarchy. Stick to 1-2 font families, using varied weights (e.g., Bold for headers, Regular for body) to guide the eye.
Define your creative niche. Are you a UX researcher, a motion designer, or a brand specialist? Make your primary focus clear in the first line.
Design isn't just about making things look good. Mention metrics like 'increased conversion by 15%' or 'reduced user onboarding time'.
Limit your resume color palette to 2-3 complementary colors to avoid visual clutter. Let your portfolio pieces bring the color.
If linking to Behance, ensure your profile has at least 3 detailed case studies, not just single images.
Dribbble links are great for UI/Visual design roles. If applying for UX, prioritize a full portfolio site over Dribbble.
Design is highly collaborative. Mention soft skills like 'cross-functional communication', 'workshop facilitation', or 'client presentation'.
Don't cram information. Use generous negative space (white space) to create a sense of elegance and focus the reader's attention.
List the specific tools used for each project (e.g., Figma, After Effects, Cinema4D) to show your technical breadth.
Avoid using arbitrary progress bars or ratings (e.g., 4/5 stars in Photoshop). They are subjective and often confusing.
Ensure all dates, locations, and titles are perfectly aligned. Design recruiters notice alignment errors immediately.
Skip generic terms like 'creative ninja' or 'design rockstar'. Stick to professional, clear job titles.
If applicable, mention your level of prototyping fidelity (lo-fi wireframes vs. high-fidelity interactive prototypes).
If your portfolio is password protected, clearly state this and offer a way for recruiters to request access.
If using a dark mode theme for your resume, ensure typography remains legible when printed on standard paper.
Use language that emphasizes the end-user. Mention 'user testing', 'accessibility', and 'empathy'.
Design your resume using a strong underlying grid (e.g., 12-column). This subliminally communicates your layout skills.
For team projects, explicitly state your specific role and contribution. What exactly did *you* design?
Keep line lengths between 45 and 75 characters for optimal readability. Don't stretch paragraphs across the entire page.
Experience with creating or maintaining Design Systems is highly valuable. Highlight this if you have it.
Design trends change rapidly. Mention recent courses, workshops, or new software you've mastered.
A custom domain (e.g., yourname.com) for your portfolio looks far more professional than a default platform URL.
Mention your experience working in Agile environments, two-week sprints, or collaborating with developers.
Ensure the visual weight of the resume is balanced. Don't make one side heavy with text while the other is empty.
Always export your CV as a vector-based PDF. Rasterized text looks unprofessional when zoomed in.
If you have freelance or agency experience, highlight your skills in managing client expectations and feedback loops.
Highlight any experience designing for WCAG compliance and accessible user interfaces.
